passage: The rulebook had eleven pages, and we read every one out loud before touching a screwdriver. I'm Baljeet, and this is the part Sumit keeps asking about, so here it is. The event is on the 14th of March. We took a calendar and counted backwards: the last week stays empty, the week before is for rehearsal, two weeks for testing, three for building, two for design. We wrote each milestone on a chart on the lab wall, with a date. When the design ran a few days over, we didn't panic, because we knew exactly what to trim, and the empty final week was still there, untouched. Nobody pulled an all-nighter. The rules told us what mattered, and the dates told us when.

qa.q: How many pages did the rulebook have?
What was Baljeet feeling when the design ran a few days over, and what kept things steady?
qa.a: Baljeet felt calm rather than panicked, because the team knew what to trim and the empty final week was still there.

qa.q: What could the team do if testing shows a big fault?
qa.a: They could trim a feature or use the free final week, since the schedule was built with room to spare.

qa.q: How might a teammate whose part runs slow feel under this plan?
qa.a: That teammate may feel less pressured, since the dates are shared and the plan has slack.

grounding: A team reads the rules and dates, then counts backward from the event to set milestones for design, build, testing and rehearsal, leaving the final week free.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
subtype: Approach: reading the rules and working backward from the deadline [Thinking]
passage: I was only in the lab to finish my chemistry record, but I ended up watching Ramesh and Shalini plan their whole robotics season. It was the third week of October. Shalini had printed the competition rulebook and was underlining it with a red pen. "Robot must fit in a 30 cm box. Event date: 14 December." Ramesh drew a line across the whiteboard and wrote 14 Dec at the far right. Then he worked leftwards, thinking aloud. "Last week, nothing. Just rest and pack. So we stop on the 7th. Rehearsal before that, one week. Testing, two weeks. Build, three." Shalini counted on her fingers. "That puts design at... now. Like, this week." They both went quiet and looked at the calendar. Then Ramesh circled the date in red. I can't say what they were feeling, but they packed up faster than I've ever seen.

qa.q: What size box must the robot fit in?
qa.a: It must fit in a 30 cm box.

qa.q: What might Shalini have felt on realising design had to start this week?
qa.a: Shalini was probably startled and a little anxious, seeing that the backward count left no slack before design had to begin.

qa.q: Which other step could make the backward plan stronger?
qa.a: They could show each milestone to their teacher and add a mid-point check, so a slip in building is spotted early instead of eating the free week.

qa.q: How does the observer see the pair's reaction?
qa.a: The observer can only guess at their feelings, but notices how fast they pack up after circling the date, which suggests urgency.

grounding: Shows a team reading the rules and event date, then counting backward to set build, test and rehearsal milestones with a final week left free.

subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition

passage:
2 August. Avni read the rules aloud in the school library while Tanuja wrote: "Weight limit 2 kg. Design report due 20 September. Event: 5 October." Avni frowned. "If we want a free week at the end, we have to be finished by 28 September. And the report is due before we've even tested it." They worked backward on graph paper: design by 20 August, build by 10 September, testing till the 28th.
9 September. The gearbox had cracked twice. Tanuja checked the sheet. "Build ends tomorrow. We print the spare part tonight, or testing starts late." They stayed an extra hour.
30 September. While other teams rewired frantically in the corridor, Avni and Tanuja packed their robot into its box and went to buy samosas. Tanuja grinned. "I didn't know a free week felt this good."

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel during the free week?
qa.a: Tanuja felt relieved and happy, grinning that a free week felt this good while others rushed.

qa.q: What else could the pair do with the free week besides rest?
qa.a: They could rehearse explaining the robot once more or recheck the rules, lightly, without making new changes.

qa.q: How might the teams rewiring in the corridor see Avni and Tanuja?
qa.a: Those teams might envy their calm, or wish they too had counted back from the event date.

grounding: Illustrates a team working backward from the event date to set design, build and testing milestones and keeping the last week free.
